If Clauses with past Perfect Form of Verb
We use the third conditional to talk about what the consequences of actions that did not occur could have been.
If we hadn't tracked the defects for this project, we wouldn't have addressed them on time.

We use the third conditional when we want to explain or point out the possible consequences of a past event that did not take place.

Different from the zero, first and second conditionals, which refer to present or future events, the third conditional talks about unreal past events or actions.

The structure of the third conditional is the following:

If clause:
If + subject + past perfect of main verb

Main clause:
subject + would/could/might + present perfect of main verb


Example:
If we had tracked the defects before, the project wouldn't have been delayed.

Note that if we invert the order of the sentences, we will not write a comma separating both sentences.

Example:
The project wouldn't have been delayed if we had tracked the defects before.
So, most of the defects wouldn't have been fixed if they hadn't been tracked?
If we hadn't looked at these patterns, we wouldn't have realized that we needed to improve the requirements' definition and coding areas.
If we hadn't compared the defects found in the testing with those found in production, we wouldn't have realized how many defects our testing processes we are not detecting.
Understanding the Concept of Defect Tracking
Defect tracking is the process in which the defects found in the program are tracked throughout the development of the project.

•	Defect tracking is the process in which logged defects are tracked from the start to the end of the project. If we hadn't tracked the defects for this project, we wouldn't have addressed them on time or even worse, we wouldn't have fixed them at all

During the course of the development of a software, there are many defects or problems that are going to appear as a result of human errors. These defects can appear for various reasons and they can be encountered from the very beginning of the project, up to the last stages.

As throughout the project the team is going to find various defects, it is very important to track them properly. This means that the defects have to be entered in a database with a clear description of what the defect is about, to whom it is going to be sent, how severe it is, etc. This process is very important because sometimes the defects are going to have to be addressed by different people in order to validate that it is effectively a defect and not only a user's error. Therefore, whoever has to analyze the defect needs to have enough information available.

To deliver a project on time, the team needs to be very organized and make sure that the defects are fixed promptly. This is why, tracking defects will help the person in charge of fixing the defect to learn about the problem as soon as possible.

Arnold: I'm still getting acquainted with software development terms and I'm not sure what defect tracking is for.
Carl: Defect tracking is the process in which logged defects are tracked from the start to the end of a project. If we hadn't tracked the defects for this project, we wouldn't have addressed them on time or, even worse, we wouldn't have fixed them at all.
Arnold: As far as I'm concerned, many organizations consider this to be an indispensable process for the development of their projects. What makes it so important?

Carl: On the course of a project, many defects are going to occur as an undeniable human error. Once these defects have been detected, they need to be tracked, usually, by using a defect tracking system in which the details about defects are entered. In this way, the information is going to be available for the other team members. Sometimes, these defects need to be validated, they're reviewed by different people and then finally, they arrive at the person responsible for fixing it. That's why it's utterly important to track defects, this is to ensure that there's clear information about how the defect should be treated.
Arnold: So, most of the defects wouldn't have been fixed if they hadn't been tracked?

Carl: Most likely. Moreover, tracking defects helps to find defect patterns that point out where most defects come from. For instance, if we hadn't looked at these patterns, we wouldn't have realized that we needed to improve the requirements' definition and coding areas.Yet another advantage of defect tracking is the improvement in models for testing. If we hadn't compared the defects found in the testing with those found in production, we wouldn't have realized how many defects our testing processes we are not detecting.
